summary: Darius Emrani, CEO of Scorecard, opens by establishing his credentials: he built evaluation systems for self-driving cars at Waymo and Uber ATG and for rockets at SpaceX, and holds patents on evaluating autonomous systems. A benchmark, he explains, is a bundle of individual evals standardizing a test set and metric across models, comparable to the SAT. These scores now control billions in market value, investment decisions, and developer mind share, so the incentives to game them are enormous. He catalogs three common manipulation tactics. First, apples-to-oranges comparisons: xAI presented Grok-3 beating competitors while comparing its best configuration against others' standard configurations, omitting OpenAI's stronger consensus-64 results. Second, privileged access to test data: OpenAI funded FrontierMath and saw the entire dataset before publicly announcing a surprising 25% score, creating a trust problem even if nothing improper occurred. Third, optimizing for style over substance: Meta entered 27 tweaked Llama-4 variants into LM Arena, one of which won with a nonsensical but emoji-filled, flattering answer; researchers showed that filtering out style effects completely changes rankings. Emrani ties this to Goodhart's Law and cites Andrej Karpathy, SWE-bench creator John Yang, and CMU's Martin Sat acknowledging the crisis. To fix public metrics, he wants like-for-like comparisons with cost-performance transparency, open-sourced test sets with no financial conflicts and regular rotation, style-controlled metrics, and all attempts made public. For practitioners, he offers a five-step framework: gather real production data, choose metrics that matter (quality, cost, latency), test the top models on your data, systematize evaluation, and iterate continuously. He closes with Scorecard's pre-deployment evaluation loop as the separator between reliable AI teams and those constantly firefighting.

takeaways: Benchmarks standardize test sets and metrics across models, making scores comparable, but billions in market value now hinge on these numbers, incentivizing manipulation.
Trick one: cherry-picking configurations, as xAI did comparing Grok-3's best setup against rivals' standard setups while omitting OpenAI's consensus-64 results.
Trick two: buying privileged access, exemplified by OpenAI funding FrontierMath and viewing the dataset before announcing scores.
Trick three: optimizing for style over substance, as Meta did with 27 Llama-4 variants on LM Arena; style effects account for significant score variance.
Goodhart's Law explains why benchmarks fail when billions are at stake: once a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
Even benchmark creators and AI leaders (Karpathy, John Yang, Martin Sat) admit the evaluation system is broken.
Public metrics need like-for-like comparisons, transparent open test sets with rotated questions, style-controlled metrics, and public attempts to prevent cherry-picking.
Build your own evaluations: gather real production data, choose relevant metrics, test top models on your data, systematize, and iterate continuously.
A pre-deployment evaluation loop separates teams shipping reliable AI from those constantly firefighting production issues.

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Background
sections.summary: Darius introduces himself as CEO of Scorecard, having built evaluation systems at Waymo, Uber ATG, and SpaceX, with patents on autonomous system evaluation. He outlines the talk: why benchmarks control billions, three ways companies game them, and how to build evaluations that work.

sections.title: What Benchmarks Are and Why They Matter
sections.summary: A benchmark bundles individual evals with a standardized test set and metric across models, like the SAT. Scores control billions in market value, investment, enterprise contracts, and developer mind share. Sona's acquisition of Auto Rover based on SWE-bench results illustrates how a single number can define market leaders.

sections.title: Trick One: Apples-to-Oranges Comparisons
sections.summary: xAI's Grok-3 benchmark graphs compared its best configuration against competitors' standard configurations, omitting OpenAI o3's stronger consensus-64 results. True performance leadership requires best-to-best or standard-to-standard comparisons.

sections.title: Trick Two: Privileged Access to Test Questions
sections.summary: FrontierMath was meant to be secret, but OpenAI funded it and received access to the full dataset before announcing a surprising 25% score. Even if a verbal agreement prevents training on the data, the optics of a company funding its own benchmark undermine trust.

sections.title: Trick Three: Style Over Substance
sections.summary: Meta entered 27 Llama-4 Maverick variants into LM Arena; one won with a nonsensical but engaging emoji-filled riddle answer over Claude's correct one. Style-controlled rankings by LM Marina changed results entirely. SAT scores show 39% of variance is essay length, illustrating the same problem.

sections.title: The Root Cause: Goodhart's Law and Expert Concerns
sections.summary: Goodhart's Law explains that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Experts including Andrej Karpathy, SWE-bench creator John Yang, and CMU's Martin Sat publicly acknowledge the evaluation crisis and broken yardsticks.

sections.title: Fixing Public Metrics
sections.summary: Fixing benchmarks requires addressing model comparisons, test sets, and metrics. Comparisons need equal computational budgets and transparent cost-performance trade-offs. Test sets should be open-sourced with no financial ties and regularly rotated. Metrics must control for style effects and require all attempts to be public.

sections.title: Five-Step Framework for Use-Case Evaluations
sections.summary: Rather than chase public benchmarks, build your own evaluations: (1) gather real production queries, (2) choose metrics that matter (quality, cost, latency), (3) test top five models on your data, (4) systematize with consistent repeatable evaluation, and (5) iterate continuously.

sections.title: Pre-Deployment Evaluation Loop and Conclusion
sections.summary: Scorecard's workflow cycles through identifying issues, building improvements, evaluating before deployment, deploying only when quality bar is met, and monitoring. This pre-deployment loop separates reliable AI teams from those firefighting. Emrani closes that all benchmarks are wrong but some are useful; measure what matters to your users, not to Twitter.

limitations: Public benchmarks are vulnerable to manipulation when billions of dollars are at stake.
Style effects in model outputs can dominate rankings, masking actual accuracy.
